Songs with 'Train' in the title.Love Train: The O'Jays' 1972 hit reached No. 1 in the US and urges all the world to join hands.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Peace Train: Cat Stevens wrote it in 1971, and it later got him into controversy after he changed his name to Yusuf.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Train in Vain: The Clash's 1979 song was hidden track on London Calling, and it was not listed on the sleeve.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Downtown Train: Tom Waits wrote it, and Rod Stewart took it into the charts in 1990.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Long Train Runnin': The Doobie Brothers' 1973 song features a famous harmonica-like guitar riff and jangling rhythm.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Night Train: James Brown's 1962 instrumental version gave a boost, and it is a title used by many R&B acts.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Mystery Train: Elvis recorded this Sun Records song in 1955, and it was first written by Junior Parker.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Runaway Train: Soul Asylum's 1992 song had a music video with images of missing children, and it won a Grammy.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Drive: The Cars' 1984 ballad was a hit, and it was used in Live Aid footage about Ethiopia, and not about a train.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Little Red Corvette: Prince's 1983 hit uses a sports car as a metaphor.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Mustang Sally: Wilson Pickett's 1966 soul hit is about a Ford Mustang, so it is about a car rather than a train.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Highway to Hell: AC/DC's 1979 title track is about road life, and Bon Scott died the following year.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Fast Car: Tracy Chapman's 1988 hit is about escaping poverty, and a car, not a train.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Born to Run: Springsteen's 1975 anthem, about escape by car, took six months to record.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Pink Cadillac: Written by Springsteen, but Natalie Cole had the hit in 1988, and it is a car song.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Route 66: Bobby Troup wrote this road song in 1946, about the highway from Chicago to Los Angeles.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Jet Airliner: Steve Miller's 1977 hit is an aircraft song, and was written by Paul Pena.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Car Wash: Rose Royce's 1976 disco hit was recorded for a film, and it has nothing to do with trains.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Low Rider: War's 1975 hit is about customised cars in Los Angeles.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Radar Love: Golden Earring's 1973 driving song is about a driver telepathically linked to a lover.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.City of New Orleans: Arlo Guthrie made Steve Goodman's song famous, and it is named for a train but contains no "train" in its title.
Songs with 'Train' in the title.The Loco-Motion: Little Eva's 1962 hit was by Carole King, and it is about a dance, not a train, though it did sound like one, and the title has no "train".
Songs with 'Train' in the title.Ticket to Ride: The Beatles' 1965 song is about a girl leaving, and lacks the word "train" in its title.

Things a soccer referee carries.Whistle: Referees often carry a spare, and the first whistles in football date from the 1870s, replacing handkerchief signals.
Things a soccer referee carries.Yellow card: Cards were invented by Ken Aston, an English referee who got the idea from traffic lights in 1966.
Things a soccer referee carries.Red card: Sent-off players can't be replaced, so their team plays a man short; the card debuted at the 1970 World Cup.
Things a soccer referee carries.Coin: Tossed before kickoff to decide who kicks off and which end to attack.
Things a soccer referee carries.Watch: Referees keep time by wrist, adding stoppage time at the end; many carry two for backup.
Things a soccer referee carries.Notebook: Used to log goals, cautions and substitutions, and also to note cards.
Things a soccer referee carries.Pencil: Pairs with the notebook to log goals and cautions, and referees often carry a spare in case one breaks.
Things a soccer referee carries.Vanishing spray: A foam that marks the wall's distance for free kicks, and disappears within a minute or so; it was invented in Brazil.
Things a soccer referee carries.Headset: A radio link to assistant referees and VAR officials, used in top-level matches.
Things a soccer referee carries.Gavel: A judge's hammer for courtrooms; referees rely on whistles and cards, not gavels, to keep order.
Things a soccer referee carries.Megaphone: Not part of the kit; referees control a stadium of thousands with a whistle and hand signals.
Things a soccer referee carries.Trophy: Carried by the winners' captain at the end, never by the referee.
Things a soccer referee carries.Medal: Medals are handed out at ceremonies after the match, and referees get one in finals but don't carry it onto the pitch.
Things a soccer referee carries.Stretcher: Carried by medics who come onto the pitch, not by the referee.
Things a soccer referee carries.Hockey stick: Belongs to a different sport; a referee has no use for one on a soccer pitch.
Things a soccer referee carries.Racket: Tennis gear, which is not part of a soccer referee's kit, though tennis umpires carry nothing like it either.
Things a soccer referee carries.Golf club: Another sport's equipment, and definitely not part of a referee's pocket.
Things a soccer referee carries.Baseball bat: Belongs to baseball; the soccer referee's tools are small enough to fit in pockets.
Things a soccer referee carries.Umbrella: Even in a downpour, referees run in the rain with no umbrella.
Things a soccer referee carries.Shovel: A groundskeeper's tool, not a referee's.
Things a soccer referee carries.Hard hat: Construction gear; the nearest a referee gets to protection is a hoped-for good set of shin guards.
Things a soccer referee carries.Lasso: A cowboy's rope for catching cattle, which is not part of a referee's gear, though the pitch does sometimes need herding.
Things a soccer referee carries.Pom-poms: Cheerleaders shake them to cheer for a team, while a referee has to stay neutral and carries none.
Things a soccer referee carries.Tuba: A brass instrument for a band, not for a referee.

Games played on a grid.Tic-tac-toe: With perfect play it always ends in a draw, and a similar three-in-a-row game was played in ancient Rome.
Games played on a grid.Battleship: Players guess coordinates on hidden grids, and the game began as a pencil-and-paper game before Milton Bradley made the plastic version.
Games played on a grid.Connect Four: A 7-column, 6-row grid with dropping discs, and it was mathematically solved: the first player can always win with perfect play.
Games played on a grid.Chess: Pieces move across 64 squares, and the number of possible games is more than the atoms in the observable universe, by Shannon's estimate.
Games played on a grid.Checkers: Also called draughts, it's played on the same 8 by 8 board, and in 2007 researchers announced it was solved as a draw.
Games played on a grid.Go: Stones are placed on the intersections of a 19 by 19 grid, and in 2016 a computer program beat a top human pro for the first time.
Games played on a grid.Sudoku: The 9 by 9 grid gets filled with digits so none repeat in any row, column or box, and there are no arithmetic skills involved.
Games played on a grid.Scrabble: Tiles go on a 15 by 15 board, and the game was invented by architect Alfred Butts during the Great Depression.
Games played on a grid.Crossword: Words interlock in a grid of white and black squares, and the first one appeared in 1913.
Games played on a grid.Minesweeper: Players click cells in a grid, and each number shows how many neighboring cells hide bombs.
Games played on a grid.Othello: Discs flip between black and white on an 8 by 8 board, and its tagline says it takes a minute to learn and a lifetime to master.
Games played on a grid.Dots and boxes: Players take turns drawing lines between dots on a grid, and whoever completes a square claims it.
Games played on a grid.Monopoly: It's played around a square track of properties, so there's no grid, and it began as a game to critique landlords.
Games played on a grid.Uno: A card game by an Ohio barber, it has no board, so no grid is used.
Games played on a grid.Poker: It's a card game, and no grid is involved, with hands ranked from a pair to a royal flush.
Games played on a grid.Charades: Acting out clues takes no board, so no grid is used.
Games played on a grid.Jenga: A tower of blocks balances on a table, with no grid, and its name is Swahili for build.
Games played on a grid.Darts: A circular board is used, divided into wedges, so it isn't a rectangular grid.
Games played on a grid.Dominoes: Tiles match their pips end to end in chains, so there's no grid to play on.
Games played on a grid.Pictionary: Drawing clues on a pad is the game, so no board grid is used.
Games played on a grid.Trivial Pursuit: Players move round a wheel-shaped board answering questions, and the game was created in 1979 by two Canadian friends.
Games played on a grid.Mouse Trap: A Rube Goldberg-style plastic contraption drops a cage on the mouse, and its board is a winding track and not a grid.
Games played on a grid.Operation: Players use tweezers to remove ailments from a patient, and the buzzer sounds when they touch the edges.
Games played on a grid.Candy Land: It was created in 1948 for kids recovering from polio, and uses a winding colored path, not a grid.

Video gamer slang.GG: Short for 'good game', GG is typed at the end of a match as a sign of sportsmanship, though sometimes sarcastically after a crushing loss.
Video gamer slang.Noob: Derived from 'newbie', noob mocks inexperienced players. It's also used to tease friends, so it can sting or be affectionate.
Video gamer slang.Respawn: When a character dies and comes back at a set point, it respawns, a blend of 'resurrect' or 'return' with 'spawn'. Respawn Entertainment took the name.
Video gamer slang.Lag: Lag is the delay between pressing a button and seeing the result online, caused by slow connections. Ping measures it in milliseconds.
Video gamer slang.Boss fight: A boss fight is a tough showdown at the end of a level. Many players say the memorable ones teach you the game's rules through pain.
Video gamer slang.Speedrun: Speedrunners finish games as fast as possible, often using glitches. Events like Games Done Quick raise millions of dollars for charity.
Video gamer slang.Nerf: To nerf is to weaken a game element in a patch. It's borrowed from the foam Nerf toys, which are soft and harmless.
Video gamer slang.Buff: The opposite of nerf: a patch that strengthens a character or item. It can also mean a temporary power-up in game.
Video gamer slang.Grinding: Grinding is repeating tasks, such as killing monsters, to gain levels or loot. It's loved by some and dreaded by many.
Video gamer slang.Level up: Gaining enough experience points moves a character up a level, often with a small fanfare and fresh abilities. It's now used in everyday speech.
Video gamer slang.NPC: Short for non-player character, a figure controlled by the game. The term has also become internet slang for people who seem to act robotically.
Video gamer slang.Loot: Loot is the treasure enemies drop. Loot boxes, random paid bundles, have drawn legal scrutiny in countries such as Belgium.
Video gamer slang.Rage quit: To rage quit is to leave a game in anger, often after losing. Some competitive games penalize it with temporary bans.
Video gamer slang.Hang ten: Surfing slang for placing all ten toes over the board's nose. It's not gaming, so it doesn't fit.
Video gamer slang.Gnarly: Gnarly is surf and skate slang for dangerous or impressive. It's from the board world, not gaming.
Video gamer slang.Fore: Golfers shout 'fore' to warn people that a ball is headed their way. It's a golf term, not a gaming one.
Video gamer slang.Howzat: A cricketer's appeal, short for 'how's that?', aimed at the umpire when the batter might be out. It's a cricket term.
Video gamer slang.Mulligan: In casual golf, a mulligan is a free do-over of a bad shot. Card games like Magic: The Gathering also use it, but it's not core gamer slang.
Video gamer slang.Nutmeg: In football, nutmegging means passing the ball between an opponent's legs. It's a soccer term, not a gamer one.
Video gamer slang.Hat trick: Three goals by one player in a game is a hat trick. The term began in cricket, where a bowler taking three wickets in a row earned a new hat.
Video gamer slang.Purl: A purl is a basic knitting stitch. It belongs to crafts, not to gaming vocabulary.
Video gamer slang.Bogey: In golf, a bogey is one stroke over par on a hole. It's a golf score term rather than gamer slang.
Video gamer slang.Deuce: In tennis, deuce means 40-40, so a player must win two points in a row to take the game. It's a tennis word.
Video gamer slang.Touchdown: In American football, carrying the ball into the end zone scores six points. It's a football term, not a gaming one.

Things that cool things down.Fridge: Modern fridges move heat rather than make cold: a refrigerant evaporates inside, absorbing heat, then releases it out the back.
Things that cool things down.Freezer: Clarence Birdseye developed quick-freezing after seeing Inuit freeze fish fast in the Arctic, giving us frozen food.
Things that cool things down.Air conditioner: Willis Carrier invented modern air conditioning in 1902 to control humidity at a printing plant, not to cool people.
Things that cool things down.Desk fan: A fan doesn't cool the air at all; it cools you by speeding up sweat evaporation from your skin.
Things that cool things down.Ice pack: Many gel packs contain a mix of water and a polymer, which stays soft when frozen instead of becoming a hard block.
Things that cool things down.Cooler box: Insulated foam, trapped air, and a tight lid slow heat, so ice inside can last for days in a good one.
Things that cool things down.Ice cube tray: The flexible-divider ice tray was patented in the 1930s, and it freed households from buying ice blocks.
Things that cool things down.Ceiling fan: Many have a summer and winter setting: reversing the blades gently pushes warm air from the ceiling back down.
Things that cool things down.Wine chiller: A bucket of ice and water chills a bottle faster than ice alone, since water touches more of the glass.
Things that cool things down.Cooling towel: Wet it and the water evaporates, drawing heat off your skin, the same principle by which sweating cools you.
Things that cool things down.Oven: It heats rather than cools, though a hot oven leaves the kitchen so warm you might wish it came with a fan.
Things that cool things down.Toaster: It makes heat, and the glowing wire elements inside reach roughly 500 degrees Celsius.
Things that cool things down.Kettle: A trap: kettles heat water, and this one boils it, so it's the opposite of a cooling device.
Things that cool things down.Radiator: Despite the name it mainly heats by convection, though a car's radiator does the opposite and cools the engine.
Things that cool things down.Space heater: It warms a small area, and cheap ones turn nearly all the electricity they use into heat.
Things that cool things down.Hot water bottle: It holds hot water, not cold, though a rubber bottle filled with ice water can double as a cold pack in a pinch.
Things that cool things down.Electric blanket: Thin heating wires woven through the fabric warm the bed, and many models switch off automatically for safety.
Things that cool things down.Hair dryer: It blows hot air to dry hair, and the cool-shot button is the only part that cools anything.
Things that cool things down.Fireplace: Most of a fireplace's heat goes up the chimney, which is why they're less efficient than they feel.
Things that cool things down.Heat lamp: Infrared lamps warm by radiation, heating objects directly, and are used in restaurants to keep food hot.
Things that cool things down.Microwave: Microwaves heat food by making water molecules vibrate, so dry or frozen foods can warm unevenly.
Things that cool things down.Slow cooker: It cooks at low heat, usually below 100 degrees Celsius, over hours, ideal for tough cuts of meat.
Things that cool things down.Hand warmer: Disposable ones heat up through a rusting reaction: iron powder reacts with air and gives off heat.
Things that cool things down.Heated blanket: It's a warming device, so it fails this category, but it works by the same electric-resistance idea as a toaster.

Things that have a spine.Book: A book's spine is the bound edge you see on a shelf, and publishers print the title there so it can be found at a glance.
Things that have a spine.Human: Babies are born with about 33 vertebrae, but the lowest ones fuse over time, leaving adults around 26 bones in the S-curved spine.
Things that have a spine.Snake: Some snakes have over 300 pairs of ribs attached to a spine of hundreds of vertebrae, which gives them their flexibility.
Things that have a spine.Fish: A fish's backbone runs from head to tail, and it flexes side to side to drive the swimming motion.
Things that have a spine.Frog: A frog has a short spine of only about nine vertebrae, and its long hip bone, the urostyle, helps it jump.
Things that have a spine.Horse: A horse's spine can't carry much weight, and a saddle spreads the rider's load over the muscles next to the backbone.
Things that have a spine.Eagle: An eagle has a bird's spine, with many fused vertebrae in the back for a stiff, strong frame that holds up in flight.
Things that have a spine.Ring binder: A ring binder's spine is where the label goes, and the rings mechanism inside lets pages be added or taken out.
Things that have a spine.Dictionary: A dictionary's thick spine often carries the span of letters, and the largest Oxford English Dictionary runs to 20 volumes.
Things that have a spine.Shark: A shark's spine is made of cartilage, not bone, and the same lightweight material gives its entire skeleton.
Things that have a spine.Whale: A whale's spine flexes up and down, not side to side as in fish, because whales descended from land mammals.
Things that have a spine.Jellyfish: A jellyfish is an invertebrate with no spine or bones at all, and it's mostly water with a simple nerve net.
Things that have a spine.Octopus: An octopus is an invertebrate, and without any bones, it can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak.
Things that have a spine.Worm: A worm is an invertebrate with a soft, segmented body and no backbone, and it uses fluid pressure to move.
Things that have a spine.Snail: A snail is an invertebrate; its shell isn't a spine but a house that grows with it, spiraling as it ages.
Things that have a spine.Spider: A spider has an exoskeleton rather than a spine, and it grows by molting, shedding its hard outer layer.
Things that have a spine.Crab: A crab wears its skeleton on the outside, and since it has no backbone, it must molt to grow larger.
Things that have a spine.Starfish: A starfish has no brain, no blood, and no backbone; its body is held by a skeleton of tiny plates in its skin.
Things that have a spine.Slug: A slug is a snail with no shell and no spine, and it moves on a muscular foot lubricated with slime.
Things that have a spine.Leaflet: A leaflet is a single folded or flat sheet, and since it isn't bound, it has no spine, unlike a book.
Things that have a spine.Flyer: A flyer is a single printed sheet with no binding, so it has no spine, and the word comes from handing them out.
Things that have a spine.Envelope: An envelope has a fold and a flap, but no spine, since spines belong to bound pages like books.
Things that have a spine.Postcard: A postcard is a single stiff card, so no spine, though it does have a front and a back for the picture and address.
Things that have a spine.Lobster: A lobster has an exoskeleton and no backbone, and it's said to be able to keep growing throughout its life.

Things you can fill with water.Bucket: Before plumbing, buckets were how households hauled water, and the phrase 'kick the bucket' may come from the pail beneath a hanged person's feet.
Things you can fill with water.Bathtub: Archimedes supposedly shouted 'Eureka!' after noticing the water rising in his bath, which gave him the key to measuring a crown's volume.
Things you can fill with water.Kettle: Most electric kettles shut off by sensing steam with a small bimetallic strip that bends when hot, so no timer is involved.
Things you can fill with water.Water balloon: A thin latex balloon can hold a surprising load because the rubber stretches evenly, but it pops fast once a weak spot thins.
Things you can fill with water.Watering can: The long spout on a watering can's rose, the perforated nozzle, spreads water as a gentle shower so seedlings are not flattened.
Things you can fill with water.Drinking glass: Glass is technically an amorphous solid, and the old myth that old windows are thicker at the bottom because glass flows is false.
Things you can fill with water.Sink: Water really can swirl either way down a sink; the Coriolis effect is far too weak, and basin shape and leftover motion decide the spin.
Things you can fill with water.Vase: A pinch of sugar or a splash of bleach in vase water slows bacteria, which is what clogs stems and makes cut flowers droop early.
Things you can fill with water.Hot water bottle: The rubber hot water bottle was patented in the 1900s, and its ribbed surface was meant to keep the heat from scalding skin.
Things you can fill with water.Ice cube tray: Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold, a puzzle called the Mpemba effect that scientists still argue over.
Things you can fill with water.Fish tank: Tap water has chlorine that harms fish, so aquarists treat it or let it stand, and a new tank must cycle for weeks to grow helpful bacteria.
Things you can fill with water.Paddling pool: Shallow paddling pools are a real drowning risk for toddlers, since a child can drown in just a few centimeters of water.
Things you can fill with water.Colander: Holes make this a trap: a colander drains water almost as fast as you pour it, so it only holds water if you plug every hole.
Things you can fill with water.Sieve: The phrase 'memory like a sieve' works because a sieve is the classic thing that cannot hold water, and the Danaids' sieve in Greek myth was a punishment.
Things you can fill with water.Fork: Forks reached Western Europe slowly; a Byzantine bride brought one to Venice in the 11th century and clergy denounced it as vanity.
Things you can fill with water.Fishing net: Nets hold fish but not water, because the mesh is far wider than a water droplet and water simply streams out.
Things you can fill with water.Wicker basket: Tightly woven wicker can be waterproofed with tar or resin, and ancient reed baskets like the one that held baby Moses were sealed that way.
Things you can fill with water.Tennis racket: Racket strings are tuned like a guitar, often at about 20 to 30 kilograms of tension, which is a lot of springiness and no water-holding.
Things you can fill with water.Whisk: A whisk works because its loops trap and fold in air, and it is the wire gaps that make it useless for holding water.
Things you can fill with water.Comb: Combs are among humanity's oldest tools, with examples from the Stone Age, and their gaps let water pass straight through.
Things you can fill with water.Grater: Graters were reportedly invented by Francois Boullier in 1540s France, intended for cheese, and their sharp holes make them leaky and painful.
Things you can fill with water.Mesh bag: Mesh produce bags dry onions and oranges because air flows freely through the weave, and the same openings let water drain.
Things you can fill with water.Lace doily: Doilies are named after a London draper, Mr Doyley, who sold light fabrics in the 1600s, and their openwork can't hold liquid.
Things you can fill with water.Slotted spoon: The slots make it a draining tool, ideal for lifting poached eggs out of water while the liquid runs back into the pot.

Things your body makes on its own.Sweat: Sweat itself is nearly odorless; the smell comes from skin bacteria breaking it down.
Things your body makes on its own.Tears: Tears contain lysozyme, an enzyme that kills many bacteria, and emotional tears contain stress hormones.
Things your body makes on its own.Saliva: You produce roughly one to two liters of saliva a day, and it starts breaking down starch before food reaches your stomach.
Things your body makes on its own.Earwax: Earwax cleans and protects your ear canal, and it comes in wet and dry types that depend on a single gene variant.
Things your body makes on its own.Mucus: Your body makes over a liter of mucus daily, mostly swallowed unnoticed, which traps germs and dust.
Things your body makes on its own.Bile: The liver makes bile and the gallbladder stores it, where it helps break fat into digestible droplets.
Things your body makes on its own.Insulin: The pancreas makes insulin to move sugar from blood into cells, and its 1921 discovery turned type 1 diabetes from fatal to manageable.
Things your body makes on its own.Adrenaline: Adrenal glands release adrenaline in a flash, speeding your heart and sharpening senses for fight or flight.
Things your body makes on its own.Melanin: This pigment colors skin, hair and eyes, and it gives some protection from sunlight by absorbing ultraviolet rays.
Things your body makes on its own.Stomach acid: Your stomach makes hydrochloric acid with a pH around 1.5 to 3.5, and a mucus layer keeps it from digesting the stomach itself.
Things your body makes on its own.Collagen: Collagen is the body's most abundant protein, making up about a third of all protein, and it is made by your own cells.
Things your body makes on its own.Red blood cells: Your bone marrow makes about two million new red blood cells every second to replace those that wear out.
Things your body makes on its own.Vitamin C: Humans can't make vitamin C, unlike most mammals, which is why sailors without citrus once got scurvy.
Things your body makes on its own.Caffeine: Caffeine is a plant chemical, made by coffee, tea and cacao to deter pests, never by our bodies.
Things your body makes on its own.Chlorophyll: Only plants and algae make chlorophyll, the green pigment of photosynthesis.
Things your body makes on its own.Fiber: Fiber comes from plants, and humans can't digest it, which is exactly why it helps digestion move along.
Things your body makes on its own.Iron: Your body can't make iron, being an element, so it must come from food. It recycles most of what it has.
Things your body makes on its own.Calcium: Calcium is an element you must eat. About 99 percent of what you hold is stored in bones and teeth.
Things your body makes on its own.Penicillin: Penicillin comes from the Penicillium mold, famously noticed by Alexander Fleming in 1928, not from human cells.
Things your body makes on its own.Nicotine: Nicotine is made by tobacco plants as a natural insecticide, not by the human body.
Things your body makes on its own.Honey: Bees make honey from nectar, and it's so stable that edible honey was found in ancient Egyptian tombs.
Things your body makes on its own.Silk: Silkworms spin silk, and legend says a Chinese empress discovered it when a cocoon fell into her tea.
Things your body makes on its own.Venom: Venom is made by snakes, spiders and scorpions. Humans have no venom glands, though a few mammals like shrews do.
Things your body makes on its own.Pollen: Plants make pollen to reproduce, and a human body doesn't, though it famously triggers sneezing.

Phobias of animals.Arachnophobia: Fear of spiders is among the most common phobias, and it affects about 3 to 6 percent of people, though most spiders are harmless.
Phobias of animals.Ophidiophobia: Fear of snakes may be inherited: studies show even babies pay quicker attention to snake images than to flowers.
Phobias of animals.Cynophobia: The word comes from the Greek kyon, meaning dog, and the fear often traces back to a childhood scare involving a bite or chase.
Phobias of animals.Ailurophobia: Ailurophobia, fear of cats, has famous sufferers: Napoleon and Julius Caesar are said to have had it, though evidence is thin.
Phobias of animals.Entomophobia: Entomophobia covers fear of insects in general, and it is a broader term than the fear of any single bug such as spiders.
Phobias of animals.Musophobia: From the Latin mus, meaning mouse, this fear of mice and rats is common, even though mice are much more afraid of us.
Phobias of animals.Ornithophobia: Fear of birds is real: people with it can panic at the flapping of wings, and Alfred Hitchcock's The Birds played on it.
Phobias of animals.Ichthyophobia: Ichthyophobia is a fear of fish, and it sometimes extends to fish on the plate or even to swimming near any fish.
Phobias of animals.Apiphobia: Fear of bees comes from the Latin apis, and it is also called melissophobia, from the Greek word for bee.
Phobias of animals.Claustrophobia: Claustrophobia is the fear of confined spaces, such as elevators or MRI scanners, not of any animal.
Phobias of animals.Acrophobia: Acrophobia is fear of heights, from the Greek akron, meaning peak, and is often confused with vertigo, which is dizziness.
Phobias of animals.Nyctophobia: Nyctophobia is fear of the dark, which is common in children and sometimes lingers into adulthood.
Phobias of animals.Aerophobia: Aerophobia is fear of flying, not of animals, even though birds do it with ease.
Phobias of animals.Glossophobia: Fear of public speaking is called glossophobia and is often ranked as one of the most common fears, sometimes above death.
Phobias of animals.Coulrophobia: Coulrophobia, the fear of clowns, targets people in costumes, not animals, and became a pop culture staple after Stephen King's It.
Phobias of animals.Trypanophobia: Fear of needles is trypanophobia, and it can cause some people to faint, since blood pressure drops at the sight.
Phobias of animals.Hydrophobia: Hydrophobia literally means fear of water, and it was an old name for rabies because victims struggled to swallow.
Phobias of animals.Agoraphobia: Agoraphobia comes from the Greek for marketplace and means fear of situations where escape feels hard, such as crowds.
Phobias of animals.Astraphobia: Astraphobia is fear of thunder and lightning, and plenty of dogs and cats seem to have it too.
Phobias of animals.Hemophobia: Hemophobia is the fear of blood, and unusually it can slow your heart and make you faint rather than speed it up.
Phobias of animals.Mysophobia: Mysophobia is fear of germs and dirt, a term coined in 1879 by American physician William Hammond.
Phobias of animals.Triskaidekaphobia: Triskaidekaphobia is fear of the number 13, which is why many buildings skip a thirteenth floor.
Phobias of animals.Pyrophobia: Pyrophobia is the fear of fire, from the Greek pyr, which also gives us pyre and pyromaniac.
Phobias of animals.Chronophobia: Chronophobia is a fear of time passing, sometimes seen in prisoners, and it has nothing to do with animals.

Things a mermaid would have.Fish tail: The fish tail is the mermaid's defining feature, and the legend likely grew from sailors spotting manatees and dugongs.
Things a mermaid would have.Seashells: Seashells are a classic mermaid accessory, and mollusks build their shells from calcium carbonate drawn from seawater.
Things a mermaid would have.Trident: The trident is Poseidon's three-pronged spear, and in art it belongs to sea gods, but mermaids in stories borrow it too.
Things a mermaid would have.Pearls: Pearls form when an oyster coats an irritant in layers of nacre, and a natural one is rare, since most are cultured today.
Things a mermaid would have.Seaweed: Seaweed is algae, not a plant, and it supplies much of the world's ocean oxygen along with its tangly mermaid hair look.
Things a mermaid would have.Coral: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called polyps, and they cover under 1 percent of the seafloor yet host a quarter of marine species.
Things a mermaid would have.Starfish: Starfish aren't fish, and many can regrow a lost arm, so scientists now prefer the name sea stars.
Things a mermaid would have.Sunken treasure: Sunken treasure is real, as the Spanish galleon San Jose, lost in 1708, is thought to hold billions in gold and jewels.
Things a mermaid would have.Sea cave: Sea caves are carved by waves pounding at weak rock, and some of them, like Fingal's Cave in Scotland, have remarkable hexagonal columns.
Things a mermaid would have.Snow boots: Snow boots would be silly in the sea, and the mermaid's world is warm shallows and cold deep waters, not drifts of snow.
Things a mermaid would have.Bicycle: A bicycle needs legs to pedal, which is exactly what a mermaid lacks, so it's out of the question.
Things a mermaid would have.Lawnmower: A lawnmower needs grass, and a mermaid's meadow is seagrass, which is a real underwater plant that grows in beds.
Things a mermaid would have.Ski poles: Ski poles go with legs and snow, and a mermaid has neither, plus water makes poor ground for skiers.
Things a mermaid would have.Hiking boots: Hiking boots need two feet, and a mermaid has a tail instead, so she wouldn't make use of any footwear.
Things a mermaid would have.Toaster: A toaster plugged in underwater would be a shock, and mermaids need no electric kitchen under the waves.
Things a mermaid would have.Knee pads: Knee pads need knees, and mermaids famously lack them, since the tail replaces both legs.
Things a mermaid would have.Rollerblades: Rollerblades are for legs on pavement, and a mermaid glides without wheels and without feet.
Things a mermaid would have.Car keys: Car keys have no use in the sea, since mermaids swim, and it's rarely wise to leave any keys underwater.
Things a mermaid would have.Sneakers: Sneakers need feet, and a mermaid's tail fin is her only footwear, a very different kind of propulsion.
Things a mermaid would have.Leg warmers: Leg warmers go on legs, which mermaids lack, but 1980s aerobics fans loved them.
Things a mermaid would have.Trousers: Trousers are for legs, and in Hans Christian Andersen's tale the Little Mermaid trades her voice for legs.
Things a mermaid would have.Socks: Socks need feet, and in the original Andersen tale the mermaid's new legs feel like walking on sharp knives.
Things a mermaid would have.Hair dryer: A hair dryer has no place underwater, and a mermaid's famously long hair simply floats and dries out in the sun.
Things a mermaid would have.Pogo stick: A pogo stick needs legs to bounce, and the toy was invented in the early 1900s, nothing a mermaid would need.

Things that have needles.Pine tree: Pine needles come in bundles, and the bristlecone pine, which can live nearly 5,000 years, keeps its needles for decades.
Things that have needles.Cactus: A cactus's spines are what we call needles, and they're modified leaves that shade the plant and cut water loss.
Things that have needles.Sewing kit: A sewing kit has needles, and bone sewing needles about 40,000 years old have been found.
Things that have needles.Compass: A compass has a magnetized needle that aligns with the Earth's magnetic field, and Chinese sailors used one around 1,000 years ago.
Things that have needles.Record player: A record player has a stylus, often called a needle, and it reads the wiggles in the groove to produce sound.
Things that have needles.Syringe: A syringe has a hollow needle, and the modern hypodermic version was developed in the 1850s.
Things that have needles.Christmas tree: A Christmas tree's needles drop if it dries, and the tradition of the tree comes from Germany, where it began in the 1500s.
Things that have needles.Knitting kit: A knitting kit has needles, and knitting dates back at least 1,000 years, with early examples from Egypt.
Things that have needles.Spruce: Spruce has short, stiff needles that grow singly, and spruce wood is used to make violins and pianos.
Things that have needles.Oak tree: An oak tree has broad leaves and acorns, with no needles, and some oaks live for over 1,000 years.
Things that have needles.Maple tree: A maple tree has lobed leaves, and its sap is boiled down to make syrup, taking about 40 liters of sap per liter.
Things that have needles.Palm tree: A palm tree has fronds, not needles, and the coconut palm is called the tree of life in tropical regions.
Things that have needles.Rose bush: A rose bush has thorns, not needles, and botanically a rose's prickles are outgrowths of the skin.
Things that have needles.Clock: A clock has hands, not needles, though a dial gauge, like a speedometer, does use a needle pointer.
Things that have needles.Ruler: A ruler has no needles, only a straight edge and markings, so you can't sew with it.
Things that have needles.Sunflower: A sunflower has broad leaves and seeds, and its head tracks the sun while young.
Things that have needles.Fern: A fern has fronds that unfurl, and ferns reproduce with spores, not seeds.
Things that have needles.Tulip: A tulip has smooth, flat leaves, and during the Dutch 'tulip mania' of the 1630s, single bulbs sold for huge sums.
Things that have needles.Hamster: A hamster has fur, not needles, though a hedgehog has about 5,000 spines.
Things that have needles.Bamboo: Bamboo is a grass, and it's one of the fastest-growing plants, with some species gaining nearly a meter a day.
Things that have needles.Willow tree: A willow tree has long slender leaves, and willow bark gave us the idea for aspirin.
Things that have needles.Turtle: A turtle has a shell, no needles, and some turtles can live over 100 years.
Things that have needles.Birch tree: A birch tree has papery bark and flat leaves, and it's among the first trees to grow back after a fire.
Things that have needles.Daisy: A daisy has petals, and its name comes from 'day's eye' because it opens at dawn.

Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.High heels: High heels concentrate body weight onto a tiny area, and on loose gravel or rock they are an ankle-sprain waiting to happen.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Flip-flops: Flip-flops have no ankle support or grip on slippery trails, and exposed toes are easy to stub on rocks.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Ball gown: A ball gown has a huge skirt that would snag on every bramble, and it's heavy when it's wet.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Tuxedo: A tuxedo is made for ballrooms, not for muddy trails, and the thin dress shoes are slippery.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Roller skates: Roller skates need smooth pavement, and a rocky trail would stop them within a few feet.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Clown shoes: Clown shoes are comically oversized, and they'd make you trip on every root and rock.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Bathrobe: A bathrobe flaps open, soaks up rain and snags, and offers no protection from the elements.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Ski boots: Ski boots are stiff and made for gliding, and walking in them is awkward and tiring.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Swim fins: Swim fins are for water, and on land they make you waddle like a duck.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Wedding dress: Wedding dresses are long and delicate, and a muddy trail would wreck one fast.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Tutu: A tutu is airy, and its stiff netting catches on branches, and it offers no warmth or protection.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Hiking boots: Hiking boots give ankle support and a grip sole, which makes them the best choice for uneven ground.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Backpack: A backpack spreads weight onto the hips, and a good one carries load far better than hand-carried bags.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Sun hat: A sun hat shades the face and neck, and it matters at altitude where UV is stronger.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Rain jacket: A rain jacket keeps you dry, and wet clothes lose heat much faster, which makes them dangerous in cold weather.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Wool socks: Wool socks stay warm even when damp, and they wick sweat away, which helps prevent blisters.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Sunglasses: Sunglasses help block UV, and glare is stronger on snow and at altitude.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Fleece: Fleece is made from recycled plastic in many cases, and it stays warm even when damp.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Sunscreen: Sunscreen is crucial at altitude, since UV exposure increases with height above sea level.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Trekking poles: Trekking poles can take a good share of the load off the knees on downhill sections.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Water bottle: A water bottle is essential, and hikers need about half a liter per hour in warm conditions.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Cargo shorts: Cargo shorts have roomy pockets for snacks, a map or a phone, and they're a hiker's favorite.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Bandana: A bandana can serve as a sweatband, sunshade, bandage, or even a pot holder.
Things you'd regret wearing on a hike.Windbreaker: A windbreaker is light and packs small, and it cuts wind chill, which can make you feel much colder.

Things in a science lab.Test tube: Test tubes are made of thin glass so they can be heated directly, and a rack holds them because their rounded bottoms can't stand up alone.
Things in a science lab.Beaker: The beaker's graduation marks are only rough guides, accurate to maybe 5 to 10 percent, so chemists switch to a pipette or burette for precision.
Things in a science lab.Bunsen burner: Named for chemist Robert Bunsen, it mixes air with gas before burning. Opening the air hole turns a smoky yellow flame into a hotter blue one.
Things in a science lab.Pipette: A pipette moves tiny measured volumes of liquid, and modern micropipettes can handle just one millionth of a liter.
Things in a science lab.Microscope: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made single-lens microscopes in the 1600s and was the first to see bacteria, which he called animalcules.
Things in a science lab.Petri dish: Named after Julius Petri, assistant to Robert Koch, who introduced it in 1887. Alexander Fleming's penicillin was discovered on one.
Things in a science lab.Centrifuge: Centrifuges spin samples at thousands of times gravity, and are used to separate blood into its parts and to enrich uranium.
Things in a science lab.Fume hood: A fume hood pulls air away from the user, drawing toxic vapors up a duct so they never reach the face of the chemist working inside.
Things in a science lab.Lab coat: Lab coats are usually white so spills are easily spotted, and they are often cotton, since synthetics can melt onto skin in a fire.
Things in a science lab.Safety goggles: Chemical splashes can damage the cornea within seconds, which is why labs pair goggles with eyewash stations for a 15-minute rinse.
Things in a science lab.Flask: An Erlenmeyer flask, with its conical shape and narrow neck, lets chemists swirl liquids without spilling. It's named for Emil Erlenmeyer, 1860.
Things in a science lab.Burette: A burette's stopcock lets a chemist add liquid drop by drop in a titration until a color change shows the reaction has just finished.
Things in a science lab.Easel: An easel holds a canvas upright for painting, and belongs in an art studio. A lab bench holds experiments flat, not a vertical canvas.
Things in a science lab.Anvil: Blacksmiths hammer hot metal on an anvil, which is a forge tool. Lab work with metals tends to use furnaces and crucibles instead.
Things in a science lab.Gavel: The gavel of a judge or auctioneer is courtroom gear. Surprisingly, U.S. judges rarely use one, which is more common in meetings and auctions.
Things in a science lab.Saddle: A saddle is horse tack. The word comes from an old Germanic root meaning a seat, and has nothing to do with a laboratory.
Things in a science lab.Trowel: A trowel is a small hand tool for gardeners and bricklayers. Archaeologists favor the pointed type for delicate digging at a site.
Things in a science lab.Pitchfork: The pitchfork is a farm tool for hay, a classic in the American Gothic painting. It is no use for scientific experiments.
Things in a science lab.Hymnal: A hymnal is a book of hymns for church services, so it belongs in a chapel rather than among beakers.
Things in a science lab.Rolling pin: A rolling pin flattens dough in a kitchen. Some bakers swear by tapered French pins that have no handles at all.
Things in a science lab.Jukebox: Jukeboxes play records for coins, and the golden age of them was the 1940s and 50s, with Wurlitzer making some of the best known.
Things in a science lab.Dartboard: A standard dartboard's number order, 20 at the top then 1, 18, 4, is arranged to punish near misses, which is often credited to a carpenter named Brian Gamlin.
Things in a science lab.Lasso: A lasso is a looped rope for catching cattle, and the word comes from the Spanish lazo. A cowboy needs one; a chemist doesn't.
Things in a science lab.Barber's pole: The red and white barber's pole recalls medieval barber-surgeons, who also did bloodletting. Red for blood, white for bandages.

Companies named after their founders.Ford: Henry Ford didn't invent the car, but his moving assembly line, from 1913, cut Model T build time from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes.
Companies named after their founders.Dell: Michael Dell started building PCs in his University of Texas dorm room in 1984, and his company sold direct to customers.
Companies named after their founders.Disney: Walt Disney won 22 Oscars personally, still a record, and Mickey Mouse was first called Mortimer in his planning.
Companies named after their founders.McDonald's: McDonald's was founded by brothers Richard and Maurice McDonald, and Ray Kroc later bought them out and spread the franchise.
Companies named after their founders.Ferrari: Enzo Ferrari ran racing teams first, and he built road cars to fund racing, with a prancing horse emblem from a WWI pilot.
Companies named after their founders.Porsche: Ferdinand Porsche designed the original Volkswagen Beetle, and his son Ferry made the first car with the Porsche name in 1948.
Companies named after their founders.Honda: Soichiro Honda started by making piston rings, and his company became the world's biggest motorcycle maker.
Companies named after their founders.Boeing: William Boeing started the company in Seattle in 1916, and it began with wooden seaplanes.
Companies named after their founders.Gucci: Guccio Gucci worked as a bellhop at the Savoy Hotel in London, and the luggage he saw inspired his Florence leather shop in 1921.
Companies named after their founders.Kellogg's: Will Keith Kellogg and his brother invented corn flakes accidentally in 1894, when wheat they left out went stale and they flaked it.
Companies named after their founders.Hewlett-Packard: Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard started the company in a Palo Alto garage in 1939, often called the birthplace of Silicon Valley.
Companies named after their founders.Apple: Apple isn't a founder's name. Steve Jobs said he chose it after a stint on an apple farm, and it also placed the company ahead of Atari in phone books.
Companies named after their founders.Amazon: Jeff Bezos named it after the river, the biggest in the world, and began selling books out of a garage in 1994.
Companies named after their founders.Google: The name is a play on googol, the number 1 followed by 100 zeros, and it isn't a founder's name.
Companies named after their founders.Nike: Nike is named for the Greek goddess of victory, and founder Phil Knight's company began as Blue Ribbon Sports.
Companies named after their founders.Starbucks: Starbucks is named after Starbuck, the first mate in Moby-Dick, and not after a founder.
Companies named after their founders.Sony: Sony's name comes from Latin sonus, sound, and sonny, a slang for a young boy, so isn't a founder's name.
Companies named after their founders.Lego: Lego comes from the Danish leg godt, meaning play well, and the company started in a carpenter's workshop in 1932.
Companies named after their founders.Samsung: Samsung means three stars in Korean, and it started in 1938 as a trading company that sold dried fish.
Companies named after their founders.Nokia: Nokia is named after a river in Finland, and it began as a pulp mill, then made rubber boots.
Companies named after their founders.Volvo: Volvo is Latin for I roll, and the name was first registered for ball bearings.
Companies named after their founders.Pepsi: Pepsi was created by pharmacist Caleb Bradham as Brad's Drink in 1893, and renamed after dyspepsia, or pepsin.
Companies named after their founders.Coca-Cola: Coca-Cola's name came from coca leaves and kola nuts, and its flowing script was drawn by bookkeeper Frank Robinson.
Companies named after their founders.Subway: Subway began in 1965 when 17-year-old Fred DeLuca borrowed $1,000 from a family friend to open a sandwich shop, originally called Pete's Super Submarines.

Computer storage media.Floppy disk: The 3.5-inch floppy held just 1.44 MB, yet its image is still the Save icon. Its hard plastic shell means it isn't actually floppy, unlike the earlier 5.25-inch disk.
Computer storage media.CD-ROM: A CD-ROM held about 650 MB, enough to replace hundreds of floppies. Its capacity reportedly was set so that Beethoven's Ninth Symphony could fit on one disc.
Computer storage media.DVD: A single-layer DVD stores about 4.7 GB, roughly seven times a CD. Its lasers use a shorter red wavelength, making data pits smaller and tighter.
Computer storage media.Blu-ray: Blu-ray uses a blue-violet laser, with a shorter wavelength than red, to pack 25 GB onto one layer. It beat Toshiba's HD DVD in the format war of 2008.
Computer storage media.Hard drive: The first hard drive, IBM's 1956 RAMAC, stored about 5 MB on fifty big platters and weighed over a ton. Modern drives hold millions of times more.
Computer storage media.SSD: Solid-state drives have no moving parts. They store data in flash memory cells, which makes them faster and quieter than spinning hard drives.
Computer storage media.USB flash drive: Flash drives arrived around 2000 and quickly killed off floppy disks. Early ones held just 8 MB, while today's can hold a terabyte in a keychain-size case.
Computer storage media.SD card: SD stands for Secure Digital. The tiny cards launched in 1999, and the write-protect slider on the side is a physical switch that tells devices not to overwrite files.
Computer storage media.Zip disk: Iomega's Zip disk held 100 MB when it appeared in 1994, a big step above floppies. It later became known for the "click of death" failure that ruined drives.
Computer storage media.Magnetic tape: Tape is far from obsolete. Many companies still back up huge data archives to magnetic tape cartridges because they are cheap per byte and stable for decades.
Computer storage media.Punch card: Punch cards stored data as holes, an idea from Jacquard's 1800s looms. Herman Hollerith used them for the 1890 US census, and his company grew into IBM.
Computer storage media.Monitor: A monitor displays information but doesn't store it. It's an output device, so when the computer is switched off, nothing remains on it.
Computer storage media.Mouse: Douglas Engelbart invented the computer mouse in the 1960s, and his first prototype was carved from wood. It's an input device, and it can't hold files.
Computer storage media.Router: A router directs traffic between networks, like your home Wi-Fi and the internet. It moves data around rather than keeping any for long.
Computer storage media.Modem: A modem converts digital signals into forms a phone or cable line can carry. The word combines modulator and demodulator, and it handles transmission, not storage.
Computer storage media.Keyboard: The QWERTY layout dates to 1870s typewriters. A keyboard is an input device, so it passes along your keystrokes without storing your files.
Computer storage media.Printer: A printer puts data on paper, but paper isn't what we call computer storage. It's an output device, even though a printout can last for centuries.
Computer storage media.Webcam: The first webcam, in 1991, watched a coffee pot at Cambridge so researchers wouldn't make a wasted trip. It captures images, but it doesn't store them.
Computer storage media.Ethernet cable: Ethernet was invented at Xerox PARC in the 1970s. The cable carries data between devices but holds none of it, so it's a connection, not storage.
Computer storage media.Joystick: Joysticks come from aviation, where a control stick steers an aircraft. On a computer it only sends movement to a game and has no memory for files.
Computer storage media.Trackpad: A trackpad senses your finger's position and gestures. It's an input device, so it passes along movements and stores nothing.
Computer storage media.Speakers: Speakers turn electrical signals into sound waves with a vibrating cone. They only play audio; the music itself lives on the storage device.
Computer storage media.Projector: A projector throws a computer's image onto a wall or screen. It's an output device, and stores nothing of what it displays.
Computer storage media.HDMI cable: HDMI carries both video and audio in one cable, and it appeared in 2003. It transmits data between devices but isn't a place to keep any.

Video game companies.Nintendo: Started in 1889 making playing cards, Nintendo became a video game giant with Mario, Zelda and Pokémon.
Video game companies.Sega: Sega, whose name is short for Service Games, made Sonic the Hedgehog and once competed with Nintendo in consoles.
Video game companies.Capcom: Capcom created Street Fighter, Resident Evil and Mega Man, and its name is short for Capsule Computers.
Video game companies.Ubisoft: This French company makes Assassin's Creed and Just Dance, and it was founded in Brittany in 1986.
Video game companies.Electronic Arts: EA publishes FIFA-turned-EA Sports FC, Madden and The Sims, and it began in 1982 treating developers like rock stars.
Video game companies.Activision: Founded in 1979, Activision was the first third-party game developer, formed by ex-Atari programmers.
Video game companies.Square Enix: Square Enix formed in 2003 when Square, maker of Final Fantasy, merged with Enix, the Dragon Quest publisher.
Video game companies.Konami: Konami makes Metal Gear and Castlevania, and it also began in 1969 as a jukebox repair business.
Video game companies.Bandai Namco: Bandai Namco is the home of Pac-Man, formed in 2005 when toy maker Bandai merged with Namco.
Video game companies.Valve: Valve created Half-Life and runs Steam, the biggest PC game store.
Video game companies.Blizzard: Blizzard made Warcraft, Diablo and Overwatch, and it began in 1991 as Silicon & Synapse.
Video game companies.Epic Games: Epic makes Fortnite and the Unreal Engine, which powers many other developers' games.
Video game companies.Atari: Atari gave the world Pong in 1972, and its name comes from a term in the board game Go.
Video game companies.Bethesda: Bethesda makes The Elder Scrolls and Fallout, and Microsoft acquired it in 2021.
Video game companies.Pixar: Pixar makes animated films like Toy Story, and it has made no major games of its own.
Video game companies.Funko: Funko makes collectible vinyl Pop! figures rather than video games.
Video game companies.Crayola: Crayola makes crayons, and it's a toy and art company, not a game developer.
Video game companies.Spotify: Spotify streams music and podcasts; it's not a game company.
Video game companies.Adobe: Adobe makes creative software like Photoshop, not video games.
Video game companies.Intel: Intel makes processors, which power games, but it isn't a game company.
Video game companies.Logitech: Logitech makes controllers and mice for gamers, but it doesn't make games.
Video game companies.Nvidia: Nvidia makes graphics cards for gaming, but it's a hardware company.
Video game companies.Cisco: Cisco makes networking equipment, not video games.
Video game companies.Oracle: Oracle is a database software firm, not a video game company.

Launched in the 1990s.Winamp: Winamp arrived in 1997, as the app that made MP3 playing trendy.

Dutch artists.Rembrandt: Painted around 80 self-portraits across his life, a record of aging in paint, and was born in Leiden.
Dutch artists.Vermeer: Delft master of Girl with a Pearl Earring and quiet light; barely three dozen paintings survive.
Dutch artists.Van Gogh: Born in the Netherlands, but he made his best-known paintings in France, where he spent his final years.
Dutch artists.Frans Hals: A Haarlem painter of laughing faces and loose brushwork, as in The Laughing Cavalier, who was Dutch.
Dutch artists.Hieronymus Bosch: Born Jheronimus van Aken; his surname comes from his hometown, 's-Hertogenbosch, and The Garden of Earthly Delights is his masterpiece.
Dutch artists.Piet Mondrian: Known for red, yellow and blue grids; his later Broadway Boogie Woogie was made in New York.
Dutch artists.M. C. Escher: His impossible staircases and tessellations, like Relativity, are favorites of mathematicians.
Dutch artists.Jan Steen: Painted messy households so well that a chaotic home is still called 'a Jan Steen household' in Dutch.
Dutch artists.Pieter de Hooch: A Delft contemporary of Vermeer, famous for sunlit courtyards and quiet household interiors.
Dutch artists.Karel Appel: A co-founder of the CoBrA movement, named for Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam, where its members lived.
Dutch artists.Henri Matisse: French, not Dutch: Matisse led the Fauvists, whose wild colors earned them the name 'wild beasts'.
Dutch artists.Peter Paul Rubens: Flemish, from Antwerp in modern Belgium, not the Netherlands, though the region's history overlaps with Dutch art.
Dutch artists.Jan van Eyck: Flemish, working in Bruges; his Arnolfini Portrait has a tiny mirror showing the whole room.
Dutch artists.Anthony van Dyck: A Flemish painter, from Antwerp, who became court painter to England's Charles I; he was not Dutch.
Dutch artists.René Magritte: A Belgian Surrealist famous for 'This is not a pipe'; he was not Dutch, which is a common mix-up.
Dutch artists.Albrecht Dürer: German, from Nuremberg, he signed his works with an AD monogram, and is known for his woodcuts and engravings.
Dutch artists.Gustav Klimt: An Austrian Symbolist best known for gold-covered paintings such as The Kiss, so he is not Dutch.
Dutch artists.Edvard Munch: A Norwegian Expressionist and painter of The Scream, so he is not Dutch, though his work is often compared.
Dutch artists.Claude Monet: A French Impressionist whose Impression, Sunrise named the movement, so he is not Dutch.
Dutch artists.Diego Velázquez: A Spanish court painter of Las Meninas, not Dutch, though his work hangs alongside Dutch masters.
Dutch artists.Hans Holbein: A German painter who portrayed Henry VIII's court in England, not a Dutch artist.
Dutch artists.Paul Klee: A Swiss-German painter who taught at the Bauhaus, so he is not Dutch.
Dutch artists.Egon Schiele: An Austrian Expressionist who died of influenza in 1918 at 28; he is not Dutch.
Dutch artists.Salvador Dalí: A Spanish Surrealist famed for melting clocks and his moustache, so he is not Dutch.

Characters in Moby-Dick.Captain Ahab: The one-legged whaling captain, who lost his leg to the white whale, drives his crew to doom through obsessive revenge.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Ishmael: The narrator opens with "Call me Ishmael" and is the sole survivor of the Pequod, floating on Queequeg's coffin.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Queequeg: The tattooed harpooner from a South Pacific island becomes Ishmael's best friend, and his coffin saves Ishmael at the end.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Starbuck: The Pequod's first mate, a thoughtful Quaker who opposes Ahab's mad hunt, gave his name to a coffee chain.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Stubb: The cheerful second mate smokes a pipe, makes jokes even while chasing whales and stays loyal to Ahab.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Flask: The short, stocky third mate treats whale-killing as a game.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Moby Dick: The great white sperm whale was partly inspired by Mocha Dick, a real white whale hunted in the early 1800s.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Tashtego: The Pequod's Wampanoag harpooner comes from Martha's Vineyard, from the Gay Head community.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Daggoo: The enormous African harpooner serves under Flask and is nearly as imposing as the whale itself.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Fedallah: Ahab's mysterious Parsi harpooner leads a secret crew of men hidden below deck and prophesies the captain's fate.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Father Mapple: The sailors' preacher delivers a sermon on Jonah from a pulpit shaped like a ship's prow.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Captain Nemo: Jules Verne's submarine commander sails the Nautilus in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas, not on a whaler.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Captain Hook: J. M. Barrie's pirate with a hook for a hand is chased by a crocodile in Peter Pan, not by a whale.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Long John Silver: The one-legged cook of Treasure Island is a different peg-legged sea character, and a smooth-talking pirate.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Jim Hawkins: The boy narrator of Treasure Island is from Stevenson's 1883 novel, not Melville's.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Robinson Crusoe: Defoe's castaway from 1719 spends decades stranded on an island, not on a Pequod whaler.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Friday: Crusoe's companion on the island is from Defoe's novel, not Melville's.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Gulliver: Swift's traveller visits Lilliput and Brobdingnag, not the Pequod's Pacific.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Captain Flint: Treasure Island's dead pirate captain is a Stevenson invention; Silver's parrot also carries his name.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Billy Bones: Stevenson's old sea dog, who dies at the Admiral Benbow inn, belongs to Treasure Island.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Captain Bligh: William Bligh was the real captain of HMS Bounty, famous for the 1789 mutiny, not a character in Melville.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Captain Smollett: Treasure Island's no-nonsense ship's captain is a Stevenson character, not Melville's.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Ben Gunn: The marooned pirate who loves cheese is from Treasure Island.
Characters in Moby-Dick.Smee: Hook's bumbling bosun in Peter Pan is from Barrie's play, not Melville's novel.

Dragons in literature.Smaug: Smaug is the fire-breathing dragon who sits on the dwarves' gold under the Lonely Mountain and is killed by Bard.
Dragons in literature.Norbert: Norbert is a Norwegian Ridgeback dragon hatched by Hagrid, though the dragon is actually female and gets renamed Norberta.
Dragons in literature.Falkor: Falkor is the white luckdragon in The NeverEnding Story, who looks more like a flying dog than a lizard.
Dragons in literature.Fafnir: Fafnir is the Norse dragon slain by Sigurd; he began as a dwarf who was transformed by his greed.
Dragons in literature.Glaurung: Glaurung is Morgoth's first dragon in Tolkien's The Silmarillion, who curses Túrin and his family.
Dragons in literature.Toothless: Toothless is the black Night Fury in How to Train Your Dragon, and Hiccup befriends him after shooting him down.
Dragons in literature.Temeraire: Temeraire is the Chinese dragon in Naomi Novik's series, in which dragons serve in the Napoleonic Wars.
Dragons in literature.Saphira: Saphira is the blue dragon who hatches for Eragon in Christopher Paolini's Inheritance Cycle.
Dragons in literature.Hungarian Horntail: The Hungarian Horntail is the Triwizard Tournament's most dangerous dragon, which Harry faces in the first task.
Dragons in literature.Shelob: Shelob is a giant spider in The Return of the King, a monster of the dark but not a dragon.
Dragons in literature.Aragog: Aragog is the giant talking spider in Harry Potter, an acromantula, not a dragon.
Dragons in literature.Buckbeak: Buckbeak is a hippogriff, half horse and half eagle, and so not a dragon despite his wings.
Dragons in literature.Fawkes: Fawkes is a phoenix, a bird that bursts into flame and is reborn, so not a dragon.
Dragons in literature.Balrog: The Balrog is a fire demon rather than a dragon, even though it has wings and fire.
Dragons in literature.Basilisk: The Basilisk is a giant serpent, often called the king of snakes, not a dragon.
Dragons in literature.Nagini: Nagini is Voldemort's pet snake and a Horcrux, a serpent, not a dragon.
Dragons in literature.Kaa: Kaa is the hypnotic python in The Jungle Book, a snake without legs or wings, so not a dragon.
Dragons in literature.Grendel: Grendel is a monster, not a dragon, though Beowulf later does fight a dragon.
Dragons in literature.Hedwig: Hedwig is Harry's snowy owl, so she's a bird, not a dragon, though Hagrid gave her to him.
Dragons in literature.Gollum: Gollum is a hobbit-like creature obsessed with a ring, not a dragon, though he lives under mountains.
Dragons in literature.Cerberus: Cerberus is the three-headed hound guarding the underworld in Greek myth, not a dragon.
Dragons in literature.Kraken: The Kraken is a sea monster from Scandinavian legend, sometimes said to drag down ships, not a dragon.
Dragons in literature.Moby Dick: Moby Dick is the great white whale of Melville's novel, a sea creature, not a dragon.
Dragons in literature.Thestral: Thestrals are skeletal winged horses visible only to those who've seen death, not dragons.

Prizes for books.Booker Prize: The UK's top fiction prize is open to English-language novels published in the UK or Ireland, and the winner gets £50,000.
Prizes for books.Pulitzer Prize: Established through Joseph Pulitzer's will, the American award first honored books in 1917; the fiction prize began in 1918.
Prizes for books.Hugo Award: Named for Hugo Gernsback, the science fiction prize is voted on by fans at the annual Worldcon convention and takes the form of a rocket ship.
Prizes for books.Nebula Award: Unlike the fan-voted Hugo, this science fiction and fantasy prize is voted on by working writers in the SFWA, and it started in 1966.
Prizes for books.Newbery Medal: This US award for children's literature has been given since 1922, and is named for an 18th-century English bookseller, John Newbery.
Prizes for books.Caldecott Medal: Named for Randolph Caldecott, an English illustrator, this American medal honors the year's best illustrated picture book for children.
Prizes for books.Carnegie Medal: The UK's oldest children's book prize, launched in 1936 and named for the Scottish-born philanthropist Andrew Carnegie, who funded libraries.
Prizes for books.Costa Book Award: This UK prize, once known as the Whitbread, rewarded books in several categories before being renamed the Costa and later ended.
Prizes for books.Edgar Award: The Mystery Writers of America honor crime fiction with a statuette of Edgar Allan Poe, which is why the prizes carry his first name.
Prizes for books.Prix Goncourt: France's top literary prize carries a symbolic prize of just ten euros, but a win can send a novel to hundreds of thousands of sales.
Prizes for books.Women's Prize: Created in 1996 after an all-male Booker shortlist, it honors the best novel written by a woman in English; the winner gets £30,000.
Prizes for books.National Book Award: The US prize has been given since 1950, and its winners are chosen by a panel of writers and awarded at a November ceremony.
Prizes for books.Oscar: The Academy Awards honor films, not books, and the statuette's official name is the Academy Award of Merit.
Prizes for books.Emmy: The name comes from 'Immy', slang for the image orthicon camera tube; the award honors television, not books.
Prizes for books.Grammy: It's named for the gramophone and honors recorded music, which is why it's not a book prize.
Prizes for books.Tony Award: Named for Antoinette Perry, it honors Broadway theater, and has no category for novels.
Prizes for books.Golden Globe: Voted by foreign journalists in Hollywood, the Globes honor film and TV, not books.
Prizes for books.BAFTA: The British Academy of Film and Television Arts gives out masks, not book prizes, though it does reward adapted screenplays.
Prizes for books.Palme d'Or: The top award of the Cannes Film Festival is a golden palm, and it is a film prize.
Prizes for books.Turner Prize: This British contemporary art award has famously gone to controversial works like Tracey Emin's unmade bed, and it is not for books.
Prizes for books.Stirling Prize: Awarded by the Royal Institute of British Architects, it is Britain's top architecture prize, and not a book award.
Prizes for books.Fields Medal: Mathematics' top honor is given every four years to mathematicians under 40, and there is no Nobel for maths.
Prizes for books.Ballon d'Or: The golden ball goes to the best footballer of the year, and was first awarded in 1956 to Stanley Matthews.
Prizes for books.Olivier Award: London's main theater awards are named for Laurence Olivier and cover plays, musicals, and opera, but not books.

Things that are usually red.Fire truck: Fire engines are traditionally red, and some departments now paint them lime-yellow because the human eye notices it more easily.
Things that are usually red.Strawberry: A strawberry is not a true berry, and the seeds on its skin are each a separate fruit.
Things that are usually red.Ladybug: The ladybug's red warns predators it tastes bad, and a single ladybug can eat thousands of aphids in its lifetime.
Things that are usually red.Stop sign: Stop signs are octagonal so they can be recognized from behind or when covered in snow, and the first US ones were black on yellow.
Things that are usually red.Cherry: Cherry red is a color name of its own, and a cherry is a drupe, a stone fruit related to plums and almonds.
Things that are usually red.Ruby: Rubies are red corundum, colored by chromium, and are among the hardest gemstones after diamond.
Things that are usually red.Blood: Blood is red because hemoglobin contains iron, and it looks darker red when deoxygenated; octopus blood is blue.
Things that are usually red.Raspberry: Raspberries are actually clusters of tiny fruits called drupelets, each with a seed.
Things that are usually red.Ketchup: Ketchup began as a fermented fish sauce from southern China, and tomatoes were added only in the 1800s.
Things that are usually red.Cardinal: Male northern cardinals are bright red, and the bird is named after the red robes of Catholic cardinals.
Things that are usually red.Rudolph's nose: Rudolph first appeared in a 1939 booklet written for Montgomery Ward by Robert L. May, with his glowing red nose.
Things that are usually red.Banana: Bananas are yellow, but there are red varieties as well.
Things that are usually red.Grass: Grass is green; its color comes from chlorophyll.
Things that are usually red.Blueberry: Blueberries are blue because of a waxy coating, though the pulp underneath is green.
Things that are usually red.Emerald: Emerald is a green gem, colored by traces of chromium and vanadium.
Things that are usually red.Sapphire: Sapphire is the blue form of corundum, which is the same mineral as ruby.
Things that are usually red.Snow: Snow looks white because light scatters off the ice crystals, though watermelon snow can have a pink tinge.
Things that are usually red.Lemon: Lemons are yellow, which is why the word is also used for a faulty car.
Things that are usually red.Pumpkin: Pumpkins are orange, and the biggest ones weigh over a ton.
Things that are usually red.Carrot: Carrots are orange today, but they were once mostly purple or yellow.
Things that are usually red.Flamingo: Flamingos are pink, not red, and get their color from their diet.
Things that are usually red.Coal: Coal is black, made from ancient plant matter compressed over millions of years.
Things that are usually red.Sky: The sky is blue because air scatters short blue wavelengths of sunlight more than red ones.
Things that are usually red.Lime: Limes are green, and they are smaller and more sour than lemons.

Foods that are spicy-hot.Jalapeño: Jalapeños rate roughly 2,500 to 8,000 Scoville units, and when ripened and smoke-dried they become chipotles.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Wasabi: Real wasabi is a hard-to-grow plant, and much of the wasabi served abroad is horseradish dyed green; its heat hits the nose, not the tongue.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Sriracha: Sriracha is named for the Thai town of Si Racha, yet the famous rooster bottle was made by Vietnamese-born David Tran in California.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Tabasco: Tabasco has been made on Louisiana's Avery Island since 1868, and the pepper mash ages in oak barrels for years.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Habanero: Habaneros can be many times hotter than jalapeños, reaching over 300,000 Scoville units.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Horseradish: Horseradish heat is released when the root is cut or grated, and fades quickly, which is why vinegar is added to lock it in.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Buffalo wings: Buffalo wings are named for Buffalo, New York, where the Anchor Bar is credited with inventing them in the 1960s.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Cayenne pepper: Cayenne takes its name from the city of Cayenne in French Guiana, and its capsaicin is used in pain-relief creams.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Ghost pepper: The ghost pepper (bhut jolokia) from northeast India was certified the world's hottest in 2007, at over a million Scoville units.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Vindaloo: Vindaloo derives from the Portuguese dish carne de vinha d'alhos, meat in wine and garlic, adapted in Goa.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Kimchi: Kimchi is fermented vegetables, usually cabbage, with chili flakes, and Seoul has a museum devoted to it.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Chipotle: Chipotle comes from the Nahuatl word chilpoctli, meaning smoked chili; it's just a smoked, dried jalapeño.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Bell pepper: Bell peppers carry a recessive gene that eliminates capsaicin, so they score zero on the Scoville scale.

Foods that are spicy-hot.Nutmeg: Nutmeg grows on the same tree as mace, and in large doses it's toxic, not just spicy.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Cucumber: Cucumber is about 95 percent water, which is why it tastes cooling rather than hot.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Banana: Bananas are mildly radioactive thanks to their potassium, though nowhere near enough to matter, and nothing like hot.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Mozzarella: Real mozzarella di bufala comes from water buffalo milk, and the name derives from the Italian for to cut.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Oregano: Oregano comes from Greek words meaning joy of the mountain, and its flavor is warm and earthy, not fiery.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Basil: Basil belongs to the mint family, and its name comes from a Greek word linked to royalty; it's herbal, not hot.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Pumpkin spice: The first Starbucks pumpkin spice latte launched in 2003 and contained no actual pumpkin until 2015; the spices are warm, not hot.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Honey: Honey can last essentially forever, and edible honey has been found in ancient Egyptian tombs; it soothes rather than burns.
Foods that are spicy-hot.Mashed potatoes: Capsaicin dissolves in fat but not water, so dairy or mild starchy foods like mashed potatoes calm a burn better than a gulp of water.

Flammable things.Kerosene: The word kerosene comes from the Greek for wax, and the fuel is the base of jet fuel.
Flammable things.Charcoal: Charcoal is wood heated without oxygen, which drives off water and gases and leaves nearly pure carbon that burns hot.

Flammable things.Sand: Sand smothers flames by cutting off oxygen, which is why fire buckets are filled with it.

Flammable things.Table salt: Table salt won't burn, though it turns a flame yellow because of its sodium.
Flammable things.Ice: Ice can't burn, but methane hydrate, nicknamed fire ice, is a real frozen substance that ignites.
Flammable things.Gravel: Gravel is stone and can't burn, which is why it's used as fire-resistant ballast on flat roofs.
Flammable things.Helium: Helium is a noble gas that won't burn, unlike hydrogen, which is why modern blimps use it.
Flammable things.Carbon dioxide: Carbon dioxide is what's left after things burn, and it's what many fire extinguishers use to smother flames.
